title: Landscape surface with trajectory: where did the search go?
summary: A surface plot of the objective with the search path drawn on it shows where an optimizer went: how it moved over ridges and valleys, where it started and where it ended. The example is the Rastrigin function, a landscape with many local minima.

media.alt: Three-dimensional surface plot of the Rastrigin function with a grid of many peaks and valleys; an amber path with dots wanders from a rose square start at the upper right down to a teal star at the lower middle.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Where did the search go?
read_the_figure.axes: x1 and x2 from -3 to 3 on the floor of the box; f(x) vertical, from 0 to about 55. The surface is semi-transparent so the path is visible.
look_at: Where does the path start and where does it end? Are both marked?
Is the path monotone downhill, or does it climb over ridges?
How many local minima lie between the start and the end?
Can you see the end marker, or is it hidden behind the surface?
as_drawn: The surface is the Rastrigin function, f = 20 + x1^2 + x2^2 - 10 [cos 2 pi x1 + cos 2 pi x2], which has one narrow local minimum near every integer pair.
The amber path has 26 points and is drawn slightly above the surface. It starts at the rose square near (2.6, 2.3), f of about 43, and ends at the teal star at the origin where f = 0.
The path is jagged: it climbs several ridges on the way (to f of about 35 at one point) rather than descending steadily, as a stochastic search does.
The end star is half hidden behind a peak in this viewing angle, which weakens the point of the figure.
read_the_figure.proves: The figure shows one search path on one landscape: that the optimizer escaped local minima and reached the global one in this run. It cannot show that it will do so on other runs or that the path is typical.
if_wrong: Start and end not marked: the reader cannot tell the direction of the search.
End marker hidden by the surface: the central claim is invisible; rotate or lift the markers.
A path drawn below the surface: the 3D occlusion misleads; draw the path on top.
must_check: path on surface: the path must be drawn on or above the surface so that it can be followed over the terrain.
start and end marked: the direction and the result of the search are its two most important facts.

terms.meaning: The graph of the objective function over the parameter space.
A point lower than all its neighbours but not necessarily the lowest overall.
The lowest point of the whole landscape; for Rastrigin it is f = 0 at the origin.
The sequence of points an optimizer visits, joined in order.
A standard test function with a grid of local minima around a single global one.

remember: Rastrigin: global minimum 0 at the origin; local minima near integers.
Hessian at the minima has curvature 2 + 40 pi^2 = 397: narrow wells.
Barrier between neighbouring wells on an axis is about 20 (f at x = 0.5).
A stochastic path need not be monotone.
Mark start and end and keep the path on top.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position in the box encodes the parameters (floor) and the objective value (height). The surface colour reinforces height; it is drawn semi-transparent. The amber line with dots is the path of the search, the rose square marks the start and the teal star the end. The legend explains the three marks.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: an optimizer is a hiker looking for the lowest valley in fog. A picture of the whole terrain with the hiker's footprints shows where the hiker went, which ridges were crossed and whether the final spot is the lowest. The three-dimensional surface also makes plain why the problem is hard: the floor is covered with many small valleys.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A 3D surface hides valleys behind ridges and the viewing angle changes what appears lowest. Heights are foreshortened and perspective distorts distances along the path. Because the surface is semi-transparent, the path can look below or above the surface when it is not. And one path is one sample: the picture cannot say how often the search succeeds.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A contour map with the path on it (a plan view) removes occlusion and keeps distances honest; add a second panel of the best value against evaluation. For many runs, plot the final points of all runs on the contour map to see how often each basin is reached.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Draw the same path on a contour map of f with the 49 integer-grid minima marked as small dots, number the first and last three points of the path, and add the objective value along the path in a side panel.

steps.title: The landscape
steps.note: On the axis x2 = 0 it reduces to 10 + x1^2 - 10 cos(2 pi x1).

steps.title: Wells and barriers
steps.note: Neighbouring wells are separated by a barrier of about 20, and the wells themselves are very narrow.

steps.title: Count of the wells
steps.note: A numerical descent from a 13 by 13 grid of starts found 45 of them, so the order of 50 is right; the edge ones are the hardest to find.

worked.title: Reading the search path from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) How high is the start and how high is the end? (2) Is the path a steady descent? (3) How many wells does a random start have to compete with, and what does a barrier of 20 imply for a descent method?

solution.text: (1) The start is at (2.6, 2.3). Evaluate the function.
The end is at the origin, f = 0, so the search reduced the value by 43.
(2) No: the path rises and falls (it reaches about 35 part-way), so the search accepts uphill moves or jumps between wells; a pure gradient descent would stay in the first well.
(3) About 49 wells. A barrier of about 20 means that a descent method needs an uphill step of that size to leave a well, as the render's path does repeatedly.

worked.answer: The start is at f of about 43 and the end at 0; the path is not monotone; there are about 49 wells separated by barriers of about 20, which a pure descent method could not cross.

analyze.q: The star at the end is half hidden. What two changes to the figure would fix it without changing the data?
analyze.hint: Marker size, elevation, a plan-view panel.

analyze.q: Why does a gradient descent started at (2.6, 2.3) not reach the origin?
analyze.hint: Each well has its own basin.

analyze.q: What does the jaggedness of the path tell you about the optimizer?

evaluate.q: One path reaches the global minimum. Is the optimizer good?
evaluate.hint: Success rate over many runs and starts.

create: Redraw as a contour map with the path overlaid and the wells marked.
Draw 20 searches and mark only the end points, coloured by whether they reached the origin.

checks.q: Why is Rastrigin hard for a gradient method?
checks.answer: It has many local minima, one near every integer point, and a gradient method stops in the first well it falls into.

checks.q: The end marker is not visible from this angle. How should the figure be improved and why does it matter?
checks.answer: Raise or enlarge the marker, change the view or add a plan-view panel; the point of the figure is that the search reached the lowest point, and that must be visible to the reader.
